prompt: A sliding-window pattern transfers from positive integers to signed integers. Which question should be answered first?

constraints: Costs are nonnegative.
The budget B is nonnegative.
The selected days must be consecutive.
The goal is maximum length under total cost B.

blocks.text: The output is one contiguous interval, and every added day can only increase or preserve total cost. Use the window in this order:

items: Advance the right boundary and add that day's cost.
While the sum exceeds B, subtract the leftmost cost and advance the left boundary; a zero cost may leave the sum unchanged, so continue until the window is valid.
Record the maximum valid length ending at the current right boundary.

blocks.text: Because costs are nonnegative, no longer valid interval with the same right endpoint can start earlier than the repaired left boundary, and each boundary moves at most n times. Prefix sums can evaluate a chosen interval but do not alone select the optimum in this linear pass; sorting destroys chronology. Negative rebates can make shrinking increase the sum and invalidate the movement proof.

messages.text: Prefix sums provide range totals but do not automatically choose optimal boundaries. They become the preferred mechanism when query volume, negative values, or another search structure changes the decision.
Sorting changes which days are consecutive and therefore changes the answer object. It becomes legal only for a noncontiguous selection problem.

feedback.reason: Nonnegative contributions make window validity repairable by forward boundary movement. The transfer depends on that sign constraint, not on the advertising vocabulary.

options.text: Sort days from cheapest to most expensive, then choose the longest affordable prefix and treat those selected days as the campaign run.
Use prefix sums because consecutive-range tasks are solved by cumulative totals, and query-time arithmetic will reveal the longest affordable run.
Use a variable window because expanding cannot reduce cost and shrinking cannot increase it; negative rebates would break this movement rule.

prompt: Daily advertising costs are nonnegative and B ≥ 0. A campaign planner wants the longest consecutive run whose total cost is at most B. Which strategy-selection rule transfers, and what boundary must be remembered?

constraints: Badge IDs arrive one at a time.
The answer is required immediately.
The question is exact, not approximate.

blocks.text: Badge IDs are merely keys. The decisive signals are incremental arrival, an answer due before future data is known, and exact membership in the current event history. For each arriving ID x:

items: Check whether x is in the seen-ID set.
If it is present, emit the duplicate alert immediately.
Insert x so later arrivals can detect it.

blocks.text: Checking before insertion distinguishes a prior occurrence from the current badge itself. End-of-event sorting could answer an offline audit but misses immediate alerts, and pointer placement has no ordered discard rule. A bounded recent-history contract would require state eviction, while approximate membership would require an explicitly relaxed correctness contract.

messages.text: This is a legal offline audit candidate but violates the immediate-answer timing. It becomes appropriate when alerts may be delayed until the full event log is available.
A sequence alone does not supply the ordering invariant needed for pointer elimination. Two pointers become useful only after an ordered relation or window contract is established.

feedback.reason: The underlying contract is online exact membership over a growing prefix. Retained seen-state supports the required answer time.

options.text: Wait until the event ends, sort all IDs, and then report duplicates.
Keep pointers at the first and latest badge because two pointers work on sequences.
Maintain a set of previously seen IDs and test membership before insertion.

prompt: A venue receives badge IDs one at a time and must immediately flag an ID that has appeared earlier in the same event. Which strategy-selection rule transfers?

constraints: Daily values are immutable.
Queries are numerous.
Each query asks for an additive date interval.

blocks.text: The surface form uses days and cash flow, but the decision contract is an immutable sequence with many additive range queries. Define P[0] = 0 and P[i + 1] = P[i] + flow[i] once; the inclusive total from day l through r is P[r + 1] − P[l] because subtraction cancels every earlier day shared by both prefixes. Sorting would destroy calendar contiguity, while a set answers presence rather than an aggregate. Updates, non-additive queries, or output requiring individual transactions would change the mechanism. The general rule is to map the new story to structure, operation, and lifecycle before reusing a strategy.

messages.text: A date set can answer whether a day exists, but not the sum over a range. It becomes useful if the query primitive changes to exact membership.
Ordering by value breaks the date interval that defines each query. Sorting becomes relevant only for value-rank or threshold questions that do not depend on original chronology.

feedback.reason: The decisive structure is a static additive range query, independent of the finance vocabulary. Cumulative state supports repeated interval totals.

options.text: Store each date in a hash set and use exact date membership as the reusable operation for computing every requested interval total.
Treat days as a static sequence, build cumulative totals once, and recover each interval by subtracting two prefixes.
Sort the daily totals by value, then answer each requested date interval from the corresponding segment of the sorted sequence.

prompt: A finance tool stores one immutable daily net-flow value for a year and must answer thousands of questions such as 'What was the total flow from day l through day r?' Which prior strategy decision transfers most directly?

blocks.text: For each ID, check membership before adding it. The set is the minimum retained history needed for arbitrary earlier duplicates. Sorting after collection cannot emit prefix answers, and limiting history to a window changes the duplicate definition.

messages.text: Binary search requires ordered state that is not present.
It delays answers and cannot satisfy the per-arrival output contract.
A duplicate may be separated by any number of intervening events.

feedback.reason: The online and no-replay contract transfers the membership-state strategy, not an offline preprocessing strategy.

options.text: Maintain a seen-ID set online, query it before insertion, then insert the current ID.
Sort the complete stream after it ends, which still answers every earlier prefix immediately.
Keep only the last two IDs because duplicate detection concerns adjacent events.
Binary-search the arrival order without maintaining sorted state.

prompt: A log stream arrives once, cannot be replayed, and must report whether each event ID has appeared earlier. Which transferred mechanism fits?

constraints: Speed is an integer in a known bounded range.
Feasibility can be checked for a proposed speed.
Greater speed never reduces completed work.
At least one speed in the range is feasible.

blocks.text: The target is not an existing element but the smallest parameter satisfying a constraint. If increasing speed cannot make completion harder, feasibility is upward-closed: insufficient speeds form a prefix and sufficient speeds a suffix. That boundary licenses half discard, while the total cost is logarithmic in the speed range times the check cost. Sorting jobs may be part of the feasibility check but does not by itself search the speed domain. The transfer boundary is nonmonotonic behaviour, such as speeds that introduce failures or discrete modes where faster can become infeasible.

messages.text: A set records which speeds were tried but provides no rule for choosing informative trials or proving untried values impossible. It becomes relevant only as memoization inside another search.

Job ordering may help evaluate one candidate speed, but it does not locate the minimum parameter without a search or derivation. It becomes complete only if a proof directly computes the optimum after sorting.

feedback.reason: The unfamiliar surface still exposes an ordered answer domain and a monotonic feasibility predicate, which is the decision boundary for binary search on answer.

options.text: Sort jobs by duration; sorting alone always reveals the minimum speed.
Prove that any speed above a feasible speed is also feasible, then binary-search the first feasible speed.
Insert tried speeds into a set and choose the smallest stored value.

prompt: A production line must choose the minimum integer machine speed that completes all jobs before a deadline. A deterministic check can decide whether a proposed speed is sufficient, and the known bounded speed range contains at least one feasible value. Which strategy-selection rule transfers?

constraints: Return the first taller building to the right.
Original street order must be preserved.
Each building needs at most one witness.

blocks.text: Street position supplies left-to-right processing order, while height supplies the strict comparison:

items: For the current building j, pop every top index i whose height is strictly smaller and record j as i's first taller witness.
Do not pop an equal height: equal is not taller, so that index remains unresolved.
Push j. The stack heights are non-increasing, and every retained index has seen no taller building so far.

blocks.text: When an index is popped, the current building is its first valid witness because every intermediate building has already been processed. Each index is pushed and popped at most once, giving amortized O(n) work. Sorting loses 'first to the right,' while an ordinary unpruned stack lacks the resolution rule. Asking for every taller building would increase output and invalidate permanent discard.

messages.text: Retaining history without a monotonic invariant provides no efficient resolution rule. It becomes useful only if another mechanism searches that history or if LIFO order is itself the output contract.
Height order does not preserve street order or nearest-right identity. Sorting becomes relevant for global rank questions rather than directional nearest witnesses.

feedback.reason: The task is a next-greater relation. A monotonic stack keeps exactly the unresolved frontier and discards entries when their first valid witness appears.

options.text: Sort buildings by height, then use adjacent taller values to determine the first greater building for every original street position.
Maintain a non-increasing stack of unresolved building indices; a taller building resolves and pops strictly shorter indices.
Push every building onto an ordinary stack and never remove anything until the end.

prompt: For each building in a street, return the first building to its right that is taller. Which prior mechanism transfers despite the new surface?

constraints: Values change after nearly every query.
Queries ask for medians, not sums.
The question tests transfer boundary, not replacement implementation.

blocks.text: The original scalar prefix-sum rule relied on two facts: the data snapshot stayed stable, and an additive total could be isolated by subtracting cumulative totals. Here almost every update makes that static array stale, and subtracting two scalar sums cannot recover the value ordering needed for a median. A richer update-aware order-statistics representation may exist, but many queries cannot make this insufficient state correct. The transfer rule is to re-check output, update model, state sufficiency, and invariant even when the new prompt uses familiar nouns.

messages.text: Query volume justifies evaluating preprocessing, but cannot make an incompatible representation correct. It becomes relevant after a legal update-aware median mechanism is identified.
Range describes the selected positions, not the aggregate or update lifecycle. The claim becomes true only when the new operation and stability assumptions match the original invariant.

feedback.reason: Transfer follows preserved mechanism and preconditions, not shared vocabulary. Frequent updates and median queries remove the static additive cancellation that prefix sums require.

options.text: Reuse prefix sums because the large query count makes preprocessing valuable, even if updates and median output change what the stored state must support.
Reuse prefix sums unchanged because the selected positions are still ranges, so the familiar range-query label is enough to preserve the original strategy.
Both the update lifecycle and the non-cancellable median aggregate differ, so the stored prefix-sum invariant cannot answer the new contract.

prompt: A dashboard asks many range questions, but values are updated after nearly every query and each query asks for the median of the current range. Why does a static prefix-sum decision not transfer merely from the word range?

blocks.text: A prefix sum answers static ranges cheaply but becomes stale after an update. A dynamic index may support logarithmic updates and queries, subject to memory and constants. Contiguity alone does not turn arbitrary online ranges into one moving window.

messages.text: Answers would use stale data unless the prefix structure is rebuilt or maintained.
Sorting values does not maintain positional range sums.
Queries can arrive in arbitrary order and refer to arbitrary ranges.

feedback.reason: The new update model changes index lifetime and maintenance cost even though the query surface still says range.

options.text: A static prefix-sum strategy no longer remains valid without rebuilds; compare a maintained dynamic range structure against update/query volume.
Keep the prefix array because the query wording is unchanged.
Use a moving window because every range query is contiguous.
Sort after every update because sorting always maintains sums.

prompt: A new domain asks thousands of range totals on immutable values, then changes the values to support frequent point updates. Which transfer boundary matters?

blocks.text: If the smallest plus largest is below C, the smallest cannot pair with any remaining value to reach C; if above, the largest cannot. The candidate is an arbitrary pair, not a contiguous range, so window and prefix-sum rules do not transfer.

messages.text: Choosing one endpoint without the complementary elimination comparison is not a complete proof.
A pair sum is not an interval sum, even when indices have a numeric order.
The output selects two values, not every value in an interval.

feedback.reason: Sortedness makes an endpoint comparison eliminate all pairs involving one endpoint in the relevant direction.

options.text: Use two endpoints; if their sum is too small advance the lower value, and if too large retreat the higher value under sorted-order elimination.
Shrink a contiguous range while its total exceeds C; pair output is a window contract.
Build prefix sums because two distinct positions always form a range.
Always choose the smallest package because it leaves the most capacity.

prompt: A new problem supplies already sorted package weights and asks whether two distinct packages sum to capacity C. Which proof transfers directly?

constraints: Weights are already sorted.
Two distinct shipments are required.
Only existence is requested.

blocks.text: The logistics vocabulary changes none of the structural facts: there is an ordered sequence, a two-element sum target, and an existence output. The lightest remaining item cannot reach the target with any smaller partner when the current maximum partner is still too small; the symmetric argument removes the heaviest when the sum is too large. Hashing and repeated binary search can be legal alternatives, but the existing order makes a single O(n) pointer pass with O(1) extra state especially direct. If one witness pair were required, the same pointers could return their current indices because the input is already sorted. The transfer boundary is lost ordering, enumeration of all matching pairs, or a relation whose comparison does not eliminate an endpoint.

messages.text: Repeated binary search is legal on sorted data but costs O(n log n) and duplicates searches. It becomes relevant when pointer monotonicity is unavailable or the query structure differs.
Hashing is a candidate, not a universal requirement. It becomes preferable when the input is unsorted, expected-time lookup is acceptable, and extra memory fits.

feedback.reason: Sorted order makes the sum comparison a safe endpoint-elimination rule, so the pair-sum invariant transfers directly.

options.text: For every shipment, binary-search its complement in the remaining sorted weights; this is the only strategy that should exploit the order.
Build a hash set because pair-sum tasks require complement lookup, even when the weights are already sorted and can support ordered elimination.
Use opposite-end pointers; a sum below C eliminates the current lightest shipment, and a sum above C eliminates the current heaviest.

prompt: Shipment weights are already sorted. The system must determine whether two distinct shipments exactly fill capacity C. Which prior strategy-selection rule transfers most directly?
